Let f(x,y)=x2−2y2, where x=ssin⁡t and y=tsin⁡s. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
ssin⁡2t−4t2sin2⁡s
b
2s2sin2⁡t+2tsin⁡2s
c
2ssin2⁡t−2t2sin⁡2s
d
2scos2⁡t−2tsin⁡2s
e
s2sin⁡2t+4tsin2⁡s
Submit

decision.explanation: Substitute to get f=s²sin²(t)−2t²sin²(s). Holding t constant, ∂f/∂s=2s sin²(t)−4t²sin(s)cos(s)=2s sin²(t)−2t²sin(2s), which is option c.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14097479/assets/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =t\operatorname{cos}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(2s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡s)(t\operatorname{cos}⁡s) \\  & =2s{sin}^{2}⁡t-4{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡s\operatorname{cos}⁡s \\  & =2s{sin}^{2}⁡t-2{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Let f(x,y)=x2−2y2, where x=ssin⁡t and y=tsin⁡s. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
ssin⁡2t−4t2sin2⁡s
b
2s2sin2⁡t+2tsin⁡2s
c
2ssin2⁡t−2t2sin⁡2s
d
2scos2⁡t−2tsin⁡2s
e
s2sin⁡2t+4tsin2⁡s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=2x,∂f∂y=−4y

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=2ssin⁡t,∂f∂y=−4tsin⁡s.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=sin⁡t,∂y∂s=tcos⁡s.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s=(2ssin⁡t)(sin⁡t)+(−4tsin⁡s)(tcos⁡s)=2ssin2⁡t−4t2sin⁡scos⁡s=2ssin2⁡t−2t2sin⁡2s.

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =t\operatorname{cos}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(2s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡s)(t\operatorname{cos}⁡s) \\  & =2s{sin}^{2}⁡t-4{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡s\operatorname{cos}⁡s \\  & =2s{sin}^{2}⁡t-2{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

−3

3
c
−6

6

decision.explanation: The chain rule gives ∂f/∂t=(2x+2y)s+6x+6z=2s²t+2s²+12st+12s−6t=2(s²t+s²+6st+6s−3t). Thus c₁=6, c₂=6, c₃=−3, and their sum is 9.

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+y+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x+y+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={e}^{x+y+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot (-1)+({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot 2t+({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot 1 \\  & =-{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}+2t{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}+{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}} \\  & =2t{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+y+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x+y+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={e}^{x+y+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot (-1)+({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot 2t+({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot 1 \\  & =-{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}+2t{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}+{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}} \\  & =2t{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}

If f(x,y)=x2+yx and y=sin⁡x, compute dfdx.

a
 2x+sin⁡x+cos⁡xsin⁡x

2x+sin⁡x+xcos⁡x

 2x+sin⁡x+cos⁡x

 2x+xsin⁡x

EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=2x+y,∂f∂y=x

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get

∂f∂x=2x+sin⁡x∂f∂y=x.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get

dydx=cos⁡x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdx=2x+sin⁡x+xcos⁡x.

content.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$
